questions.question: How does the SKIP status differ from FAIL in Robot Framework execution reports?

options.text: SKIP indicates tests that were intentionally not executed, while FAIL indicates tests that ran but had errors
SKIP and FAIL are equivalent; SKIP is just the modern name for FAIL
options.explanation: SKIP and FAIL are distinct statuses with different meanings

options.text: SKIP means the test passed but was marked for future review
options.explanation: SKIP indicates the test was not executed, not that it passed

options.text: SKIP is used for tests that failed due to timeout, while FAIL is for assertion errors
options.explanation: Both timeouts and assertions result in FAIL; SKIP means not executed

questions.question: What does the SKIP status indicate?

options.text: That a test|task was explicitly skipped during execution
That a test|task failed but the failure was ignored
options.explanation: SKIP indicates the test was not executed, not that a failure was ignored

options.text: That a test|task passed but with warnings
options.explanation: SKIP means the test was not executed, not that it passed with warnings

options.text: That a test|task is scheduled for future execution

options.text: Only in a separate skipped tests report

questions.question: Which are valid reasons to use the SKIP status?

options.text: Temporal exclusion of tests|tasks for known issues until resolved
Conditional execution based on runtime conditions
Marking tests|tasks as unsupported in certain environments but keeping them in logs
Hiding failed tests from reports to improve success rate
options.explanation: SKIP is not for hiding failures; it's for legitimate reasons to not execute tests

questions.question: Why is --skip better than --exclude for documenting that a test was not executed?

options.text: Because --skip allows the test to be re-enabled easily

options.text: Because --exclude causes errors in reports while --skip doesn't
